problem: Learned active-perception systems add hand-designed sensing proxies (coverage, curiosity, reconstruction) that can conflict with the task, and moving the sensor to novel viewpoints hurts learned encoders calibrated to a fixed viewpoint distribution, so gaze exploration is punished before it helps.
motivation: On hazardous terrain, hazards and the goal may lie below, beside or behind the robot, so a limited-FOV camera must decide where to look before deciding where to go. The value of information is unobservable at decision time, and the paper asks whether a separate sensing objective is needed at all, or whether task reward alone can make gaze emerge.
key_idea: Train a single policy that commands both body twist and pan-tilt camera velocity with a progress-only reward, on a gaze-invariant egocentric belief-map representation and a spawn-distance curriculum, so that gaze control emerges from task pressure alone.
insight: Gaze is task-driven: the GT-oracle variant, with identical camera control and free maps, lets the gaze atrophy into a gimbal corner, so learned gaze exists only because the policy relies on the belief it feeds. Sweep (scripted scanning) loses to Active (74.2 vs 92.7) because of timing: belief maps forget in about 1 s and indiscriminate scanning wastes time, even hurting on pillars (75.0 vs Passive 97.7). Passive collapses (2.5 on crests, 5.8 on islands) where hazards lie below a level gaze, showing the value of gaze is terrain-dependent.
method: POMDP formulation: state includes base pose, pan-tilt, goal and terrain; the goal is never observed except through the camera; the reward depends only on body position (no sensing term).

Reward: potential-based progress from a geodesic cost-to-go φ (Eikonal/Bellman, slope + clearance cost, feasibility from Δh_max=0.4 m and body-width dilation), plus success bonus, fall penalty 2.5 and time cost. Probe-and-return detours net zero progress, so gaze earns reward only via progress.

Gaze-invariant belief maps: depth is back-projected by fixed geometry into yaw-aligned egocentric maps, fine (0.1 m, 3.2 m) and coarse (0.6 m, 19.2 m), with 5 channels (height mean/std, ray count, goal-hit count, visitation), evidence decay and diffusion. The maps act as memory in place of a recurrent state.

Transformer asymmetric actor-critic: a 3-layer encoder over 66 tokens (belief patches, GT-map patches, CLS from robot state, CRITIC from privileged terrain vector); the attention mask hides privileged tokens from the actor. The action is a 4-D unicycle twist plus pan-tilt velocities.

Spawn-distance reverse curriculum: per-environment difficulty d_i places the spawn along the waypoint chain from the goal, increasing on success and decreasing on struggling failure; five procedural terrain families (islands, crests, pillars, bridges, decoys) are designed so hazards are not visible from a level forward gaze.

Fast GPU depth ray-caster: Taichi 2D DDA over heightmaps with skip maps, 11.5x faster than the IsaacLab ray-caster, enabling on-policy training with depth for 4096 envs; PPO for 900M steps (about 20 h on an A100).
Locomotion stage: a separate Go2 locomotion policy (50 Hz joint targets) tracks the 10 Hz twist commands, and its height scan is sampled from BM_fine at test time; sim2sim transfer to MuJoCo.

setting.backbone: 3-layer Transformer encoder (ViT-style patch tokens) trained from scratch with PPO; separate RL locomotion policy for Go2
setting.training_data: RL in a custom GPU-parallel simulation on procedurally generated heightmap terrains (5 families, 900M steps), with a curriculum and no external data
setting.observation: Egocentric depth (200x116, RealSense D435 model) on a pan-tilt mount integrated into fine and coarse belief maps, plus robot state (past actions, velocities, camera direction, height, gravity)
setting.action_space: Continuous unicycle twist (v in [-0.3,1.5] m/s, yaw rate up to 1.5 rad/s) plus pan-tilt velocities (up to 0.9 rad/s), executed by a locomotion policy
setting.simulator: Custom Taichi GPU heightmap environment (training); MuJoCo full-body Go2 (sim2sim transfer)
setting.privileged: none at test time for LEAP (the GT and CRITIC tokens are zero-filled and masked); the GT oracle variant gets ground-truth maps, and the locomotion scan reads GT heights within 1 m of the spawn

numbers.bench: other:Hazardous-terrain goal navigation (planar sim, 5 procedural families)
numbers.eval_set_note: 5 seeds x 4 episodes x 100 unseen layouts per terrain type (2,000 episodes per terrain-variant pair), spawn at d=1
numbers.extra: mean±std over 5 seeds; success by geodesic cost-to-go < 0.5 m

numbers.bench: other:Hazardous-terrain goal navigation (planar sim, 5 procedural families)
numbers.backbone: same Transformer with attention to GT tokens

numbers.bench: other:Hazardous-terrain goal navigation (planar sim, 5 procedural families)

numbers.eval_set_note: 5 seeds x 20 layouts x 6 episodes = 600 episodes per terrain and variant, d=1

numbers_note: Success per terrain is stored under SR_<terrain> keys; the Robustness-to-spawn-distance figure gives only qualitative curves. No standard VLN/ObjectNav benchmarks.
results: LEAP reaches 92.7% mean held-out success, versus 74.2% for scripted Sweep and 34.5% for Passive, within 4.6 points of the GT oracle (97.3%). In MuJoCo full-body transfer the ordering GT > Active > Sweep > Passive holds (94 / 92 / 79 / 38 mean).
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation on procedural 2.5D heightmap terrains (no overhangs, no real robot); the navigation-locomotion interface is frozen and the policies are trained separately.
Weaker at near-goal spawns (small d), where goal discovery needs steep upward gaze that is rarely practiced, causing timeouts.
The sim2sim success rates are not comparable to the planar rates, and results cover only synthetic hazard families.
builds_on: Perceptive locomotion elevation mapping (Miki et al.)
